judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: 'The menfolk of [Place] cannot live without us!' and the grumbling Ogre stomachs are classic Nox deadpan. The hint about a secret passage tells the player what to do in one plain line.

items.label: B
items.critique: The two asks don't connect, and the button-pusher's 'You must be good luck!' is pleasant but generic. 'Basic training isn't for everyone' feels like a modern idiom.

items.label: C
items.critique: The sponsorship-for-a-favour chain is neat and plausible, and the refusal leaves a clear 'where to find me'. It is tidy, with little of the campaign's oddness.

items.label: D
items.critique: Breathless 'Sir! Help me please!' openers and a stammered 'Could you... would you get it back for us?', with near-identical 'token of my appreciation' thanks: the repetition Westwood never minded.

items.label: E
items.critique: A blunt guild master who quotes a price, 'And you are sent by the Captain, eh?', and a gruff beast-seller ('Ya want one?'). These are short trade lines with stated gold amounts, as in the campaign.

items.label: F
items.critique: The 50,000-gold inn sale is a joke stretched over four lines, and the farewell ('I hope you survive this whole mess... stay out of [Person]'s way if you want to stay alive!') runs longer and chattier than Nox's shopkeepers.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'It's not easy running a smuggling ring, you know' and 'Good luck with whatever business you're up to!' have a sitcom wink. The outcomes are long strings of thanks plus item plus warning plus thanks again.

items.label: H
items.critique: The bounty with capture and kill outcomes at different prices, 'young sir' throughout, 'I'll lose no sleep fretting about his soul!' and '--' before the gold: very much the campaign's register.

items.label: I
items.critique: It shares the bounty lines with H, and the innkeeper's robbery ask and 'filthy paws on our belongings!' payoff fit the same voice and price-stating habit.

items.label: J
items.critique: The used-car-salesman patter ('only used it on weekends', 'I like your face') is a familiar modern bit, and the four lines all turn on one sales joke rather than telling the player much.

tells: New texts lean on recognisable modern comic bits (the used-car sale, the sitcom smuggler, the absurd property price) and spread one joke across every line. Westwood's humour is a single deadpan beat inside a functional line.
New outcomes chain several clauses (thanks, item, warning, thanks again, good luck). Westwood outcomes are shorter and front-load the reward.
Westwood repeats stock phrases ('token of my appreciation', 'young sir', '--' before a sum) without embarrassment. The new texts vary their phrasing more.
Pairs of asks that don't relate to each other or to the town read as assembled. Westwood's pairs usually belong to one situation or one speaker type.
Modern idioms ('isn't for everyone', 'whatever business you're up to', 'this whole mess') stand out against Westwood's slightly formal, archaic-tinged plainness.
